**159 newsrooms and desks; 144 carry a send address, 138 of those mechanically confirmed on the page that publishes them. 74 are tier 1.**

9 of those addresses are marked **not a news inbox** — the outlet publishes no editorial address and this is its only published route (a general org inbox, an opinion desk, membership support, in one case a site administrator). They are kept because they are the way in, and flagged because a press release sent to one as though it were a city desk is a misfire. Write those as a short personal note, not a release.

Compiled 2026-08-30 for the launch release. Press contact `press@overberg.co` / 312-718-4318; the volunteer ask goes to `hello@overberg.co`.

## The release

Written by a reporter, not generated. It is pasted VERBATIM beneath every pitch; only the one personal line above it changes per outlet.

> What state house district do you live in? What's your police district? You might know your school board district? But what about the Illinois Supreme Court districts?
>
> When trying to get something done in your community, one of the first things you need to know is the right person, agency or jurisdiction to talk to. And for any given U.S. resident, that can mean anywhere from a handful to two dozen districts that cover their address.
>
> "I was at a community organizing event, and I was talking with a neighbor about a project. Then we realized that, even though we lived near each other, we were actually in two different districts. But that's often not easy to figure out," explains Adam Overberg, cyber security expert and creator of districtry.com.
>
> That's how the project was born.
>
> Overberg began by combing through government websites to get map layers and geographic boundaries for local, county, state and federal districts in Chicago. It was at times cumbersome - there's no standard organizational system for this type of government data across agencies.
>
> Then he expanded to New York and San Francisco, and now has coverage of nearly all counties in Illinois, Wisconsin and Iowa.
>
> Districtry is an independent project. It is not a government service and is not affiliated with, endorsed by, or operated by any government agency. There is no account, no sign-in, and it never asks for personal or financial information.
>
> What it does do is tell you what districts you're in, who your elected representatives are and where to go to get the answers you need about your community.
>
> All you have to do is pick a point or enter an address and it reports every civic boundary that contains it at once - legislative, judicial, policing, schools, and the local special districts that most tools leave out.
>
> The app names who holds each seat, according to the latest available data, and links the official body when none does. Districtry never guesses an officeholder.
>
> Because Districtry is open source and transparent, every layer names the publisher of the data. Every line of code in Districtry is public.
>
> So what comes next? Overberg says he wants to continue building out the app, eventually creating a resource for every major city and all 3,143 counties in the U.S. But that's a heavy lift, as much of this work is done by manually finding datasets, sometimes calling agencies and then unifying that data into the Districtry platform.
>
> How can I help? - Get the word out. Share Districtry with a friend, or on social media. Use the tool! You can also donate your time and resources. Do you want your community represented? Contact Districtry at hello@overberg.co and ask how you can get involved in gathering data.
>
> Overberg sees this project highlighting the problem with how geospatial district-level data is stored across government agencies. He says he wants to use this tool to bring attention to the lack of consistent record keeping, and bring about legislative change in Illinois and beyond for how local, county, state and federal bodies keep and update this type of information.
>
> For more information about the project, interview requests or access to shareable or embeddable versions of Districtry, please contact Adam Overberg at press@overberg.co or 312-718-4318.

## How this file is used

The same rules `docs/ASK_DRAFTS.md` sets for outbound asks apply here, for the same reason:

1. **The operator sends. Nothing here is sent automatically, and no pitch is sent by the agent that compiled the list.** A cold e-mail to a newsroom is outward-facing and cannot be recalled; it goes when a person decides it goes.
2. **Record the send date the day it goes, never before**, in the ledger at the foot of this file. An unsent row and a sent-but-unanswered row are different states and must not look alike.
3. **One follow-up, at 6–8 business days, in the same thread, carrying something new.** Then stop. A newsroom that did not bite is a closed question, not a queue.
4. **One address per message. No BCC, no mailing-list tool.** A visible blast to thirty tips inboxes is a filter event, and it is also the thing that makes a sender a spammer rather than a correspondent.
5. **A clean no is a good outcome** and worth recording — it closes an outlet for good.

## How each address got here

Two independent steps, because a wrong address does not merely fail — it burns the pitch and, if it bounces to a shared desk, the sender's name with it.

* **Researched under a no-guessing rule.** The agents that compiled this were forbidden from inferring an address from a pattern — no `tips@`, no `news@`, nothing reconstructed from a domain. Every address had to be read on a page the agent actually fetched, and returned with that page's URL and a verbatim snippet showing it published there.
* **Then re-checked mechanically.** `scripts/verify_press_list.py` re-fetches every cited page and looks for the address on it, decoding Cloudflare `data-cfemail` obfuscation and PDF text along the way — both of which had already produced false misses here, and one of which (Cloudflare) is the same trick that once silently emptied seven county e-mail addresses out of this project's own data.

So the **State** column is a measurement, not a confidence:

| State | Means |
|---|---|
| `confirmed` | the address was found on the page cited for it |
| `BOUNCED` | mail to it was rejected. It is left on the list, struck, so nobody tries it again. |
| `markup-only` | the address is on the cited page but ONLY inside machine-readable markup — JSON-LD, a meta tag, a data attribute — and in no text or `mailto:` link a reader ever sees. **This is the shape the Chicago Tribune's dead address had.** Nobody at the outlet looks at it, so nobody notices when it dies. Treat as unconfirmed. |
| `unrechecked` | that page refuses this network (Akamai/Cloudflare 403, a TLS failure). **This is a fact about the host, not a doubt about the address** — the same inversion `validate_card_links.py` uses for its `EXPECTED_UNREACHABLE` hosts. Confirm in a browser before sending. |


**And a limit worth stating plainly.** PUBLISHED IS NOT DELIVERABLE. Every address here was read on a page that publishes it and then re-checked by fetching that page again. Neither test can tell you a mailbox still accepts mail — outbound SMTP is not available to the tooling, so no address here has been proven deliverable. The Chicago Tribune bounce on 2026-09-01 is what taught this: newsroom@chicagotribune.com was published, and had been dead long enough that nobody noticed, because it appeared ONLY in the page's schema.org JSON-LD. `risk: markup_only` marks the addresses that share that shape — present in machine-readable markup but in no text or mailto link a reader ever sees. Treat those as unconfirmed and expect some to bounce.

Rows with **no send address at all** are listed separately. They are not failures: a newsroom that publishes only a form is answered through its form, and several sites here sit behind a captcha or a managed challenge that nothing in this repo will route around.

## Where the release goes, and in what order

Every link is tagged `utm_campaign=districtry-launch` and `utm_medium=email`, with a per-wave `utm_source`, so the whole push totals as one campaign while each room splits out. That tagging is the only attribution that will ever exist for most of these sends — and it is checked: the app reads `utm_*` before the hash router strips them (`il/index.html`), and a `utm_source` other than `share`/`embed` renders the landing page rather than forwarding, so a Wisconsin editor clicking a root link is not silently dropped into the Illinois app.

### Wave 1 — The school board hook (Chicago, hand-written)

*Day 1 (a Tuesday), 6:30–8:00am CT, all ten out before 8:15*

**Subject:** A free lookup for Chicago's new school board districts (54 chars)

**Opens:** On November 3 Chicago elects its first fully elected school board, ending 30 years of mayoral control: one member in each of 20 subdistricts, plus a president elected citywide. districtry.com/il tells any resident which subdistrict they vote in from a typed address — free, no account, no ads, no tracking. The same lookup returns every other district containing that point: ward and alder, police district and beat, CPS attendance zone, park and library district, state House and Senate, and judicial subcircuit.

**Who:** Ten sends, one per outlet, each written by hand: Chalkbeat Chicago (the anchor), Block Club Chicago, WBEZ / Chicago Public Media, Chicago Sun-Times city desk, South Side Weekly (one send covering the Hyde Park Herald), City Bureau / Documenters, Illinois Answers Project, WTTW News / Chicago Tonight, City Cast Chicago (Hey Chicago newsletter), Chicago Public Square. Every address is the outlet's own published tips/news desk; a current byline is named in the first line, never in the To: field.

**Why this order:** This is the only pitch in the whole send with a date attached. A rebrand is not a story; 'the school board subdistrict you vote in this November, from your address' is — and this is the first election in which every seat is on the ballot. Ten is the honest ceiling for one person writing genuinely different emails before 8am, and these ten are the rooms where a school-board lookup is on-beat rather than a curiosity — Chalkbeat and Block Club most of all. Say 20 subdistricts, never 21: the 21st seat is the citywide president, which no district lookup can answer.

### Wave 2 — Chicago metro breadth, plus six specialist swaps

*Day 2, 6:30–8:00am CT for the specialists; the templated block sent 9:00–11:00am CT the same day, split into two batches with a gap*

**Subject:** Every district your block is in, from ward to police beat (57 chars)

**Opens:** A single Chicago address sits inside about a dozen districts at once — ward, police district and beat, elected school board district, park, library and fire district, township, state House and Senate, congressional, judicial subcircuit — and each is published by a different agency in a different format. districtry.com/il returns all of them from one typed address, free and with no account or tracking, and every layer names the agency its boundary came from.

**Who:** About 37 sends. Hand-written specialists (7): Injustice Watch (judicial subcircuits — almost nobody else covers them and the app has the layer), Streetsblog Chicago (wards, precincts, park districts and streets), Crain's Chicago Business (one unfunded builder, civic tech), Invisible Institute and CWBChicago (police districts and beats), Chicago Daily Law Bulletin and Illinois Lawyer Now (circuit courts and subcircuits).

**Why this order:** The neighborhood, community and language weeklies are the rooms most likely to actually run it, because 'which districts cover our blocks' IS their beat — but they need the ward/beat/precinct framing, not the school-board one, so they cannot ride wave 1's letter. The specialists get hand-written subjects because each has exactly one layer nobody else covers, and naming that layer is worth more than any amount of general description.

### Wave 3 — Illinois beyond Chicago: 91 counties, and the 11 that aren't

*Day 3–4, 6:30–8:00am local; the wire and association sends held to Day 4, 2:00pm CT (locals get first look)*

**Subject:** 91 of Illinois's 102 counties — and the 11 that aren't (54 chars)

**Opens:** districtry.com/il now answers for 91 of Illinois's 102 counties, rebuilt one county at a time from each county's own maps, certified canvasses and, in a few cases, a phone call to the clerk. It also states plainly which counties it still cannot answer for and why — that list is the story, because no two Illinois counties publish their district lines the same way.

**Who:** About 27 sends. Morning, one per outlet with a real county list: Capitol News Illinois, Capitol Fax, NPR Illinois (WUIS), IPM Newsroom / WILL, WGLT, WCBU, WSIU, WNIJ, The News-Gazette, Journal Gazette & Times-Courier, The Southern Illinoisan, Shaw Local News Network, Belleville News-Democrat, Illinois Times, The State Journal-Register, The Pantagraph, Herald & Review, Peoria Journal Star, Rockford Register Star, Quad-City Times / Dispatch-Argus, Effingham Daily News, St. Louis Post-Dispatch, Jacksonville Journal-Courier, WCIA, WICS, Telegraph Herald (one send, covering its Iowa/Illinois/Wisconsin tri-state footprint including Jo Daviess).

**Why this order:** Downstate desks do not care that a Chicago app exists; they care whether it answers for their counties. The merge field here is genuinely reportable and costs nothing because the repo already publishes it: name the served counties in that outlet's footprint, then name the unserved ones and why.

### Wave 4 — The complete states, and the two cities

*Day 8 (the Tuesday after the holiday-shortened week) for Wisconsin and Iowa; Day 9 for NYC and San Francisco. 6:30–8:00am in each outlet's own time zone*

**Subject:** All 72 Wisconsin counties, mapped to who represents you (55 chars)

**Opens:** districtry.com/wi covers all 72 Wisconsin counties from a typed address — county supervisory districts, municipal wards, school districts, state Assembly and Senate, and the rest — free, no account, no tracking. Completeness is the part worth checking: Illinois took county-by-county work to reach 91 of 102; Wisconsin is 72 of 72, and Iowa is 99 of 99 counties with one gap I did not create: Jones County is missing from the Iowa Legislature's own statewide supervisor-district file, so the lookup says so there rather than guessing.

**Who:** About 45 sends across four templates. Wisconsin (20): Wisconsin Watch, Votebeat Wisconsin, Wisconsin Examiner, Urban Milwaukee, Milwaukee Journal Sentinel, PBS Wisconsin / Here & Now, Milwaukee Neighborhood News Service, The Capital Times, Wisconsin Public Radio, Wisconsin State Journal, Green Bay Press-Gazette, Leader-Telegram, Wausau Pilot & Review, WXPR, Racine County Eye, TMJ4, Milwaukee Courier, City Cast Madison, Wisconsin FOI Council, Wisconsin Newspaper Association.

**Why this order:** This is a different and bigger claim than Illinois's, and it must not be sent in Illinois's letter: Wisconsin is 72 of 72 and Iowa is 99 of 99 counties with one stated hole — Jones County is absent from the Iowa Legislature's own statewide supervisor-district file, so that one county gets no supervisor card — which a statewide editor can check in thirty seconds by typing their own address, and that is exactly why it lands. STATE THE HOLE IN THE PITCH: an editor who finds it themselves has caught you overclaiming; an editor you told has been handed the story. NYC and SF are single-city instances, so their hook is their own unit of government (community districts; supervisor districts), not coverage arithmetic.

### Wave 5 — The national trade, the policy problem, and the ask

*Day 10–11, 8:00–10:00am ET; newsletters and listservs sent at least two days before each one's own stated publication day*

**Subject:** 262 counties, and no two publish districts the same way (55 chars)

**Opens:** I rebuilt civic district boundaries for 262 counties across Illinois, Wisconsin and Iowa, and the hard part was never the geometry — it was that no two counties publish the same thing the same way. Some serve an ArcGIS layer, some a scanned PDF, some only certified election returns, and a few answer only by telephone.

**Who:** About 27 sends. Trade and gov-tech: StateScoop, Government Technology, Route Fifty, Governing, Smart Cities Dive, Bloomberg CityLab, Geo Week News, NACo County News. Elections and democracy: electionline Weekly, Democracy Docket, Bolts Magazine, Stateline, Ballotpedia, The Fulcrum. Data and accountability: MuckRock, The Markup, 404 Media, The 74. Newsletters and roundups: Civic Tech Field Guide, Maps Mania. Association letter, not a news pitch (7): NSGIC, Geospatial Professional Network, ILGISA, IACCR, Illinois State Bar Association's Illinois Lawyer Now if not already sent in wave 2, NICAR-L, Chi Hack Night.

**Why this order:** The policy angle — that there is no standard for how a local body publishes and updates its geospatial district data — is the strongest thing the project has to say to a national audience, and it is only credible AFTER the local waves, because the evidence for it is the county-by-county record the earlier waves generate.

## The data desk

Chris's note, 2026-09-02: **address the data reporter or data editor where an outlet has one.** For a pitch whose entire subject is a dataset nobody had assembled, they are the reader who knows immediately why 91 counties took months. Every person here was read off the OUTLET'S OWN staff or author page and every address comes from that page's own markup — none is inferred from a firstname.lastname pattern, which is the one thing the research rules forbid outright. The send still goes to the desk; the data reporter is who the first line names.

24 across 18 outlets; 16 publish a personal address, 8 do not (reach those through the outlet's desk address above and name them in the first line).

**Measured absences.** A page that loaded and does not name a data desk is an answer, not a blank — it is what stops the next pass re-probing the same page.

- **Block Club Chicago** — NO DATA DESK — measured 2026-09-02. The full team page renders (103 role words: 51 reporters, 46 editors) and the word 'data' appears ONCE, 'graphics' never. This is an absence on a page that loaded, not a page that failed.
- **Chicago Tribune** — NO DATA BYLINE OBTAINABLE — measured 2026-09-02. The Tribune publishes no staff directory (already recorded above) AND its author pages state no job title at all, so there is no Tribune page that says who its data desk is. Aggregators (Muck Rack, Feedspot, SignalHire) claim to know; they are scraped contact brokers and this list does not cite them.
- **Injustice Watch** — NO DATA DESK — measured 2026-09-02. Its 'Visual Reporter' creates visual ART for stories; that is illustration, not data journalism.
- **KQED** — HAS a data desk (Lisa Pickoff-White, Data Journalist and Senior Producer) but publishes NO address for her: the staff page's payload carries one beside "display_author_email": false. Found by the mechanical check flagging it MARKUP_ONLY — the same class as the Tribune's dead newsroom@ — and dropped, because an address the publisher switched off is not a published address.
- **The San Francisco Standard** — NO DATA JOURNALIST — measured 2026-09-02. Its staff page does carry 'Senior Data & Analytics Manager' and 'Senior Data Engineer', which are business and engineering roles, not newsroom ones. A data title is not a data desk.

## Send mechanics

- INDIVIDUAL SENDS ONLY. No BCC, no CC, no mailing-list tool, in any wave. One address per message, even for the 30 templated sends in wave 2 — a newsroom tips inbox filters visible-blast mail, and a BCC header is the single fastest way to be read as a PR shop rather than a person. If a send tool is used at all, use it for one-to-one delivery with no list headers and no unsubscribe footer.
- PERSONALIZATION PAYS IN EXACTLY THREE PLACES, and nowhere else is worth the hours: (1) naming the ONE layer the outlet already covers — subcircuits to Injustice Watch, beats to Invisible Institute and CWBChicago, wards-and-streets to Streetsblog, school board to Chalkbeat; (2) naming the counties in a regional outlet's own footprint in wave 3, served and unserved, taken from docs/COUNTY_STATUS.md so it is verifiably true; (3) a clickable permalink to a real address inside that outlet's coverage area with the relevant layer switched on. Everything else — the description of the app, the ask, the signature — is a clean shared template and should not be reworded per outlet.
- PERSONALIZATION DOES NOT PAY on the wave 5 trade and newsletter block, or on the wave 4 out-of-state templates beyond swapping the state's own numbers and unit of government. Those readers want one tight paragraph and a working link; a fake-personal opener ("I loved your piece on…") from a stranger reads worse than a plain one.
- DEEP-LINK EVERY PITCH TO THE READER'S OWN TURF. The app takes permalinks of the form https://districtry.com/il/?utm_source=press-chi-schools&utm_medium=email&utm_campaign=districtry-launch#point=41.8825,-87.6285&layers=school-board — query first, hash last. Give each Chicago neighborhood weekly a point on its own main street, each downstate daily a point in its county seat, each NYC/SF outlet a point in its coverage area. An editor who clicks a link that opens on their own block does not need the rest of the email.
- UTM PER WAVE, one campaign: utm_campaign=districtry-launch throughout, utm_medium=email, and utm_source= press-chi-schools (wave 1), press-chi-metro (wave 2), press-il-regional (wave 3), press-fleet-wi / press-fleet-ia / press-fleet-ny / press-fleet-sf (wave 4, one per template), press-national (wave 5). That is the only tracking in the send.
- NO TRACKING PIXELS, NO READ RECEIPTS, NO LINK-WRAPPING SERVICE. This project publishes a privacy page that names every recipient of a reader's data; a pitch that opens with that claim and carries an invisible open-tracker is indefensible if anyone looks, and reporters do look. The UTM parameter on a link the recipient chooses to click is the whole measurement budget.
- ADDRESS RULE, from the plan and non-negotiable: send to the desk, tips or news inbox the outlet publishes for inbound news. A named reporter is a BYLINE TO ADDRESS THE PITCH TO in the first line ("For [name], who covers [beat] —"), not a To: field, unless that outlet publishes that reporter's address on its own staff page. Re-open every contact page the week of its wave and re-copy the address; a wrong address burns the pitch and there is no second first impression.
- DE-DUPE BY ADDRESS BEFORE SENDING, NOT BY OUTLET NAME. The verified list contains the same room twice under different names — South Side Weekly and South Side Weekly (with the Hyde Park Herald); City Bureau / Documenters and City Bureau / Chicago Documenters; Austin Weekly News under two entries plus Wednesday Journal, all Growing Community Media; WTTW twice; Capitol News Illinois four times; Wisconsin Public Radio, KCRG and electionline twice each. One inbox receiving two pitches in two waves is a spam signal that costs the outlet, not just the message.
- PLAIN TEXT, UNDER 200 WORDS, NO ATTACHMENTS. The release is a link, not a PDF; a 200KB attachment from an unknown sender is a filter event at most newsrooms. Structure every letter the same: two-sentence lede (the story), two sentences of what it does and who built it, one line of what it is not (no account, no ads, no tracking, not a government service, not affiliated with any agency), one link, one three-item offer, signature.
- CLOSE WITH A THREE-ITEM OFFER, identical across waves: a 10-minute call, a screen recording or screenshots on request, and a data check for their coverage area ("send me any address in your circulation and I'll tell you what it returns and what it can't"). The third one converts regional editors, because it is a free fact-check of the tool they are being asked to write about.
- TWO ADDRESSES, TWO JOBS. press@overberg.co with 312-718-4318 in the signature block; hello@overberg.co appears once, in the final line, as the volunteer ask. Do not put the volunteer ask in the subject or the lede — it dilutes a news pitch into a recruitment mail.
- DELIVERABILITY BEFORE WAVE 1: confirm SPF, DKIM and DMARC all pass for overberg.co, send test messages to a Gmail, an Outlook and a Yahoo account and check they land in the inbox, and keep total daily volume under about 40 with no more than ~25 in any 60 minutes. A solo domain going from near-zero to 150 cold sends in ten days is a reputation event; the waves are sized for that as much as for the newsroom calendar.
- SEND WINDOWS: Tuesday through Thursday, 6:30–8:00am in the RECIPIENT's local time (wave 4 crosses three time zones — schedule, don't batch). Never Friday afternoon, never Monday for wave 1, and do not let any wave land in the holiday-shortened week; that is why waves 1–3 sit in week one and waves 4–5 wait for the Tuesday after. TV desks (WTTW, NBC 5, CBS 2, WCIA, WICS, KCRG, KWWL, TMJ4, PBS Wisconsin) need the morning send and a visual — offer the screen recording explicitly to those nine.
- ONE FOLLOW-UP, EVER, at 6–8 business days, in the same thread, three sentences, and it must carry something NEW — a county that shipped since, a gap that closed, a link to that outlet's own turf. Never "just bumping." After one follow-up, stop; the project's own ask discipline is follow up twice then record it unresponsive, and press is not owed more patience than a county clerk. Anyone who replies leaves the sequence immediately and gets a hand-written thread.
- RUN THE GATES THE MORNING OF EACH WAVE, before the first send: python3 scripts/validate_index.py il/index.html, python3 scripts/validate_card_links.py, and the smoke test against the instance that wave points at. Then hand-check three to five real addresses inside that wave's coverage area. An editor's first act is to type their own address; a dead card or a stale roster on that click ends the pitch and the relationship.
- KEEP A SEND LEDGER, one row per outlet: address used, wave, date sent, follow-up due, reply, outcome. Record the send date the day it goes out, never in advance — the same rule docs/ASK_DRAFTS.md applies to county asks, and for the same reason: a silent send is not a closed one, and in three weeks you will not remember which of two Austin Weekly entries you actually mailed.
- LANGUAGE PRESS (La Raza, Lawndale News / Noticiero Bilingüe, Korea Times Chicago, Dziennik Związkowy, Chicago Chinese News, El Tecolote, El Diario NY): write in English, and state plainly what the interface's language support actually is rather than implying translation exists. Offer them the underlying boundary data for their own maps — that is a real, honest offer and it is more useful to them than a link.
- ASSOCIATIONS AND COMMUNITIES GET A DIFFERENT LETTER, NOT A PRESS PITCH. NSGIC, the Geospatial Professional Network, ILGISA, IACCR and the two press associations are asked to circulate to members or to host a talk; NICAR-L gets one short, list-norm-compliant post from a member, no marketing language, and Chi Hack Night gets a request to demo on a Tuesday, not a release. Sending a press release to a listserv is the one move in this plan that can generate an actual public complaint.
- DO NOT: offer an embargo (there is no news event to embargo), offer an exclusive to more than one outlet (offer none — the plan forbids the theatre and a discovered double-exclusive is unrecoverable), claim or imply any government affiliation or partnership, cite user numbers, traffic, or 'growing community' figures that don't exist, or describe the tool as official, authoritative or legally reliable. The release and every pitch carry the same disclaimer the app does.

## What could go wrong

- THE SCHOOL-BOARD HOOK'S CIVIC FACTS ARE THE HIGHEST-COST ERROR IN THE SEND. Wave 1's first sentence asserts something about this November's board election, to education reporters who cover exactly that. Verify the seat count, which districts are on the ballot, and the date against the Chicago Board of Election Commissioners' own published page before the wave, and state only what that page states. A project whose entire pitch is accuracy cannot open with a wrong ballot fact to Chalkbeat.
- AN EDITOR TYPES THEIR OWN ADDRESS FIRST, AND THAT IS WHERE IT BREAKS. A wrong district, an empty roster card or a dead source link on that one click ends the pitch. Mitigate by running the gates and spot-checking addresses in each wave's footprint the morning of, and by naming the gaps in the email before the reader finds them — being first to say what is missing is the whole credibility position.
- A WRONG OR STALE ADDRESS BURNS THE OUTLET, not just the message. Desk inboxes get retired, weeklies change hands (Growing Community Media / NEWSWELL, Schneps, Lee), and a bounce or a wrong-person forward means the next pitch from this domain is already spam. Re-verify every address the week of its wave, and never use a reporter address that the outlet does not itself publish.
- DELIVERABILITY FAILURE IS SILENT. If DMARC is misaligned or the domain is cold, 150 messages land in junk and the campaign reads as 'nobody was interested' rather than 'nobody saw it'. There is no bounce for a spam-foldered message; check authentication and inbox placement before wave 1, not after wave 3's silence.
- A FRONT-PAGE HIT CAN BREAK THE SITE AT THE EXACT MOMENT READERS ARRIVE. The app depends on third-party geocoding (Photon, Nominatim) and CARTO's domain-and-quota-keyed basemap tier; a Block Club or WBEZ link can exceed a tile quota or trip a geocoder's usage policy, and the app then looks broken to every reader the story sent. Know the quotas and the fallback behaviour before wave 1, and watch them on the mornings after each wave.
- REGIONAL EDITORS MAY READ 'MISSING COUNTIES' AS 'NOT FOR US'. Champaign, Ford and Piatt are all unserved in the News-Gazette's own footprint; Jasper in Effingham's, Pope in the Southern Illinoisan's, Christian in Illinois Times' and the SJ-R's, Bureau in Shaw Local's, Henderson near the Quad Cities.
- A WIRE PICKUP CAN SUPPRESS THE LOCAL ORIGINALS. AP, Lee Enterprises and the press associations reach the same desks the regional wave is pitching; if they move first, a local editor sees the story as already covered. Holding the wire and association sends to the afternoon of day 4 is deliberate and should not be optimised away for convenience.
- DUPLICATE ENTRIES IN THE LIST WILL PRODUCE DUPLICATE SENDS. At least eight rooms appear twice under different names across waves. Two pitches from one sender in ten days to the same tips inbox is a spam report risk, and it is the kind of sloppiness that a project selling data discipline cannot afford to display in its own outreach.
- MAIL-MERGE FAILURE IN WAVE 3 IS PUBLIC AND EMBARRASSING — a raw token in a subject line or a county list pasted from the wrong outlet, sent to 27 editors. The county merge is the most valuable and the most fragile part of the send; build it by hand from docs/COUNTY_STATUS.md, proofread all 27 as a batch before any of them go, and remember the county list moves as counties ship weekly, so regenerate it the day of the wave rather than reusing week-old text.
- ONE PERSON, A PUBLISHED PHONE NUMBER, AND FIVE WAVES. A TV desk that bites wants same-day; a wave sent at 7am generates calls all day. If the operator cannot clear the mornings after waves 1, 2 and 4, the fastest-moving opportunities are the ones that get missed, and an unreturned call from a metro desk is not offered twice.
- A STORY MAY DESCRIBE IT AS AN OFFICIAL OR GOVERNMENT LOOKUP. Put the not-a-government-service line in the pitch body as well as the release, and correct any published piece that implies affiliation, promptly and in writing — that correction is cheaper than the first time a reader treats a card as legally authoritative.
- THE POLICY ANGLE CAN OVERSHOOT INTO ADVOCACY FRAMING the project has not earned. 'Wants to drive legislative change' is true and should be stated as the developer's own aim; it should not become 'campaign', 'coalition', or a claim that any legislator, agency or association is engaged, because none is named in the release and a trade reporter will ask who is.
